articles.text: A request has been forwarded to us, coming from Mr. John Hager, of Mandan, to call a convention for next Saturday, for the purpose of electing a delegate to the Democratic convention at Pierre, on the 14th of the present month. Morton county intends sending a delegrte to Pierre and Billings county can appoint a delegate and send the proxy to the Morton county delegate. Although our political preferences are for the Republican party, we take pleasure in publishing this call as both parties should be organized here. Billings county is entitled to one delegate and it will be a simple matter for several Democrats to take the lead in deciding the place of meeting, etc. If the delegate does not wish to attend the Pierre convention the proxy could be sent to Mr. Hager, who would doubtless see that it is put into the hands of the Morton county delegate.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy publishes John Hager's call for a Billings county Democratic meeting to choose a delegate to the Pierre convention of May 14.

articles.text: An editor who perverts the meaning of another is as guilty as one who steals articles without giving proper credit. In last week's issue we used the words, "There is now no doubt that every pound of Black Hills freight will be shipped via Medora," meaning the words, as every sensible person can see, by the use of the word "will" to apply to the future, say a week or two hence. The present editor of The Dickinson Press, with a bungling use of tenses says: "The truth is contrary to his statement," meaning that it is not the truth at the present time. If the editor pro tem will go back to "first principles" and brush up his grammar he will see that he has either misstated himself or that he has said what he knows every one even in Dickinson believes to be false. If a solitary ray of hope had existed in Dickinson of shipping any freight after we get started why was it not brought out in the consolation meeting held by the citizens of Dickinson on the evening of April 22? The Press stated only the fact that the meeting was held, when it is known as well here as in Dickinson, that all hope was then given up of shipping any further freight from there. As is well known here and also in Dickinson, every merchant in the Hills, except three, have pledged themselves to ship via Medora. These three will stick to the Pierre route. We can hardly see what is left for Dickinson to ship except wind.
articles.summary: Packard rebuts The Dickinson Press, insisting Black Hills merchants have pledged to ship via Medora and that Dickinson has given up hope of the freight.

articles.text:
F. B. Allen, attorney for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., returned Monday morning from his Black Hills trip in company with E. Deffebach, of Spearfish. The return trip was made in a leisurely manner, with no changes and occupied three days. Mr. Allen has delayed his return till this time as he wished to thoroughly examine the mineral wealth and other resources of the Hills. The following interview is especially interesting reading, as it shows what a valuable country can be made tributary to Medora through the means of a railroad from this point:

Mr. Allen states that after reaching the divide, clear to the Hills is a first-class agricultural country. This has been so well described by Dr. Louthan in a former issue, that but little more need be said on the subject. From a point twenty-five miles north of the Belle Fourche to the base of the mountains is already very well settled. In former years the whole country was irrigated, but during the last few years the ditches have been useless as there has been ample rain. This is doubtless due to the well-demonstrated fact that much more rain will fall on the same ground after cultivation than before. In the district above mentioned more than enough grain is raised to supply the wants of the Hills, and here especially will an outlet be valuable, as it will furnish a ready market at advanced figures to these farmers. To illustrate the abundance of grain, oats are now selling at twenty-five cents and wheat at forty-five cents a bushel.

The Hills themselves are noted only as a mining region and they may well be as the half cannot be told of their fabulous resources. Mr. Allen has been in a large number of mining camps, but all of them are vastly inferior to the Hills. The gold ore is mostly of low grade but easily worked. The Homestake Co., the largest in the world, can work ore yielding only $2 a ton at a profit. The monthly clean-up of this mine averages over $3,000,000 and millions of dollars have been declared in dividends. There are hundreds of mines as valuable as the Homestake, but they are undeveloped as the cost of transporting machinery is so great. Among the undeveloped mines are those of the Carbonate Co., said to be very rich.

The silver mines are situated at Galena, the principal one being the Sitting Bull. According to the testimony of experts, brought out in the trial now going on between the Richmond Mining Co. and the Sitting Bull, there is exposed ore to the value of $500,000. All indications point to the existence of numerous other mines equally as valuable in the immediate vicinity. The Sitting Bull mine is the only one that is worked to any extent and is the sole property of Mr. Davy. He began the work and the ore was freighted to Cheyenne. By this costly method enough money was obtained to develop the mine. Competent authorities state that the mine is capable of clearing $1,000 a day.

The coal region is in Wyoming, about twenty-five miles from Deadwood. It is owned by the Philadelphia Coal Co. and as far as developed shows two veins four and six feet thick. It is similar to the Bull Mountain coal and is the best lignite yet found. The coal beds are supposed to cover about 3,800 acres.

Tin ore has been found in Bear gulch and other localities. The specimens assayed show about five per cent. The mines, owing again to the cost of transporting machinery, are as yet undeveloped, but there is no doubt tin exists in paying quantities.

Adjacent to the coal fields are situated the largest salt wells, capable of furnishing 200 tons of salt per diem. The Sitting Bull mine now derives all its salt from these wells.

Springs here also show evidences of petroleum. Mr. Allen now has a bottle of the oil and a piece of sandstone so strongly saturated with the oil that it readily blazes when a lighted match is applied to it. Oil springs are also found in the southwestern part of the Hills, beyond the located wells.

The gypsum mines of the Hills are also very valuable. The mineral is extensively used for lime and plaster of paris. Large deposits are found in the foot-hills, the veins being fifteen to twenty feet in thickness.

Veins of mica are also found in the southern hills and are being worked as extensively as is allowed by the poor facilities afforded.

From the above it can be readily seen that the Black Hills country is probably the richest in the world and all it needs for full development are better facilities for transportation. With a good railroad the country would rapidly settle up and the Medora & Black Hills R. R. is waited for even more anxiously by the people of the Hills than it is here.
articles.summary: F. B. Allen, back from the Black Hills with E. Deffebach, describes the Hills' farmland and mineral wealth and the value of a Medora & Black Hills railroad.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES.
articles.text:
The Northern New Mexico Stock Growers' Association, which met recently at Springer, represents 600,000 cattle and $25,000,000 to $30,000,000 capital.—[Western Rural.

During the winter a great many cattle from the Yellowstone range strayed across the river on the ice to the Crow reservation. Stockmen complain that the Indians kill the cattle and wantonly destroy more than they can eat, generally taking only the tongues and unborn calves.—[Billings Post.

Several persons have mentioned the fact that especially at Fargo the stock yards are entirely unfit for the reception of cattle, unloaded for feed and water. The mud is six to eight inches deep and scores of cattle die in the pens. This is a condition of things that should be remedied immediately. The stock interest is too valuable to the railroad to be allowed to suffer thus.

The shipments of live stock over the Northern Pacific R. R. the last two weeks have been greater than at any time in the history of the road. Although not many cars have unloaded at Medora, a large number will arrive during the summer and be driven upon the ranges in the Bad Lands. The Custer Trail Cattle Co., W. N. Thompson & Co., Wadsworth & Co., Niemela Cattle Co. and several others will increase their herds from 1,000 up. Several new men will also come in with large herds.

An exchange says of lambs that although they are supposed to be tender things there is no young animal that has so much vitality as a lamb, if it only has plenty of food and can get it. Very often it needs help to reach the teat and to get the milk. The ewe's teats are often closed with a gluey, sticky substance, which should be forced out and the milk started; then, if the lamb is held to the teat it will come to, when it has seemed past hope, and in a day or two will skip, if it can get but a ray of sunshine to start it.

The committee on foreign relations has agreed to report favorably to congress several amendments to the bill providing for the inspection of meats for exportation. One amendment provides that when in the president's judgment it shall be necessary for the protection of animals in the United States against infectious or contagious diseases, he may by proclamation suspend the importation of all or any class of animals for a limited time, and may change, modify, revoke or renew such proclamation as the public good may require.—[Western Rural.

The tendency of thoroughbred stock to deteriorate when turned upon the range to rustle for their feed is well understood. This suggests a point that stockmen must decide upon sooner or later. Will they buy fine stock from the breeding farms of the old states, turn them loose upon their ranges till they have survived their usefulness and then replace them with others from the same source, or will they breed their own sires and care for them as they should be cared for—that is, make a proper provision for them in the way of food and shelter?—Exchange.

The Stockman thinks there are but few, if any, industries that are more promising at the present time than breeding and raising horses. There is no danger whatever of an over-supply and prices have held firmer for the past five years on horses than on any other class of live stock, that is, for anything like first-class animals. The horse, of any merit, if placed upon the market now, need not want long for a buyer at a good round price. Nothing need stand in the way of any farmer making his horse stock yield him a good income each year, if properly handled. One advantage in having an income from a source like this is that the time when horses sell the best and when they naturally come into the market is in the spring time of the year, just the time when farmers need the money the worst and when they generally have but little of the products of the farm to sell. A few young horses can be ready for the market each spring with but little extra cost.—[Glendive Times.

Since the hides taken from the dead cattle on the range in the vicinity of Sun river have begun to come in, cattle men have concluded the loss will be somewhat larger than anticipated. Hon. R. S. Ford, who is one of the largest stock owners, thinks the loss will not fall much below ten per cent. but that the fine weather which we are now having will more than make up that loss by adding to the crop of calves, many of which die from cold, snow and wind storms, usually during March and April and this spring there will be no loss from that source.—[Livingston Enterprise.
articles.summary: Range news: northern New Mexico stockmen, Crow reservation cattle losses, Fargo stock yards, record N.P. live-stock shipments and herds coming to the Bad Lands, horse raising, and Sun River winter losses.

articles.text: Asel Keyes, one of the Northern Pacific forwarding company which controls the recently established freight route from the Northern Pacific to the Black Hills, was on the Pacific express to-day bound for Missoula and will return in a few days and visit Livingston. He says, reports to the contrary notwithstanding, the freighters have centered upon Medora as the point from which all freight for the Black Hills will be received from the railroad.—[Livingston Enterprise.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Livingston Enterprise: Asel Keyes of the Northern Pacific forwarding company says freighters have centered on Medora for Black Hills freight.

articles.text: Dakota has more post-offices than Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Idaho, Indian Territory, Louisiana, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Utah, Washington Territory or Wyoming, more than Delaware, Nevada, Rhode Island and Montana combined.—[Cooperstown Courier.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Cooperstown Courier on the number of Dakota post-offices.

articles.text:
THE BAD LANDS COW BOY is the best paper west of Fargo, except Kit Adams' daily. The editor of THE COW BOY goes out and kills a bear every morning before he attacks his raw steak.—[Minneapolis Hotel Gazette.

The editor of The Gazette doesn't appreciate the "odorousness" of comparisons and exceptions in some cases.
articles.summary: Reprint of the Minneapolis Hotel Gazette's teasing praise of The Cow Boy, with Packard's reply.

articles.summary: Work on overhauling and enlarging the abattoir will soon begin.

articles.text: The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
articles.summary: The Senate holds the Far West cigar agency.

articles.text: R. J. Jewell has returned from his eastern trip. As yet, he is undecided about his future occupation.
articles.summary: R. J. Jewell back from the east.

articles.text: C. F. Ellison, who put up the company's ice here and at Miles City, has been in Medora for several days.
articles.summary: C. F. Ellison, the company's ice man, in Medora.

articles.text: The outfit which Moody and Cummings will accompany on an eastern trip is expected here this evening.
articles.summary: Outfit for Moody and Cummings' eastern trip expected.

articles.text: Harriman, who is on his walk from Duluth to San Francisco, will probably pass through here Saturday.
articles.summary: Long-distance walker Harriman expected Saturday.

articles.text: Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
articles.summary: Roberts & Co. given sole Far West cigar agency.

articles.text: Part of the office furniture of Keyes & Bramble has arrived and the forwarding firm will be ready for business in a few days.
articles.summary: Keyes & Bramble forwarding office nearly ready.

articles.text: Although it has not been measured, a trip over our route will convince anyone that it is not over fifteen miles to the divide.
articles.summary: Route to the divide said to be under fifteen miles.

articles.text: About one hundred tons of hay were sold the last week by the company to E. G. Green, superintendent of the N. P. R. R. stock yards.
articles.summary: Company sold 100 tons of hay to E. G. Green.

articles.text: The work of grading Main St. began this morning. It will be levelled and filled in. It will vastly improve the appearance of the town.
articles.summary: Grading of Main Street began.

articles.text: We have heard nothing as yet from outside nines wanting to play us a game of base-ball. There is a good nine here just spoiling for the fray.
articles.summary: Medora base-ball nine seeks a game.

articles.text: E. Deffebach, of Spearfish, is still with us and it is to be hoped that his stay will be a permanent one. "Bassie" makes the kind of a citizen we need here.
articles.summary: E. Deffebach of Spearfish still in Medora.

articles.text: The dance given by Geo. Fitzgerald last Saturday night was a complete success. Every thing passed off pleasantly, and we hope to have more of such entertainments.
articles.summary: Geo. Fitzgerald's dance a success.

articles.text: W. B. Milne of the Minneaplis firm of Wyman, Mullin & Van Dyke, made us one of his periodical visits last Saturday. As he is a good salesman, he is building up a large trade.
articles.summary: Salesman W. B. Milne visits.

articles.text: Disgusted Cœur D'Aleners still continue to pass through on their way east. A few of them go in the cars, but the most of them, on account of the beautiful weather, prefer riding on the bumpers or trucks.
articles.summary: Disappointed Coeur d'Alene miners pass east.

articles.text: Mr. Allen returned to Bismarck Tuesday morning. He is a welcome visitor and we hope to see him often. He says that the only thing about his trip to the Hills that he didn't like is that he could only spend four cents while there and that was for postage.
articles.summary: Mr. Allen returns to Bismarck.

articles.text: Mr. Gunn, of Colorado, left for the east Tuesday. He will return soon and probably go into the cattle business in the Bad Lands. He has been a cattle man for nearly thirty years and is abundantly able and experienced to handle a large herd successfully. We hope soon to number him among our ranchmen.
articles.summary: Colorado cattleman Gunn may ranch in the Bad Lands.

articles.text: We never knew a paper that didn't contain a notice stating that old papers were for sale at the office. As we dislike following a practice that never yields a dollar a year, we wish to state that we have several bundles of papers at our office which we will give to our subscribers, if they will take the trouble to take them away. Don't think you are imposing on us by taking them, as they are of more use to any one else than to us.
articles.summary: Old papers free to subscribers.

articles.text: M. J. Conners, of Spearfish, has been in Medora for several days. He is on the way to his Beaver creek ranche, where he has about 9,000 head of cattle. Some time ago in riding all through the heart of his range he found only one carcass. His cow-boys state that more cattle died last summer than during the winter and place the total loss at less than one per cent. Mr. Conners himself said that two per cent is an outside figure. This is a remarkably fine showing, the best we have yet heard. All cattle men unite in saying that the loss in the Bad Lands especially has hardly been large enough to account for deaths from natural causes.
articles.summary: M. J. Conners reports tiny winter losses on his Beaver creek range.

articles.text: This is the last issue of THE COW BOY that will be sent to any but paying subscribers. We have given ample notice to all delinquents and we propose to have a list upon which there is not a solitary deadhead. As we have said before, a failure to receive the paper will be the best kind of an intimation that it takes money to subscribe for THE COW BOY. Three months is a long enough time for any one to pay up in. We will give this time to subscribers who are reliable, but beyond this we won't trust Vanderbilt or Gould. We are prompted to this decision by several reasons. First, cash or short credit is the only business way of running a paper. Second, we consider a money equivalent is received by subscribers just as much as if a person has a $2 bill changed into small coin. Third, we don't propose to deadhead or be deadheaded. Cash both ways will give far better satisfaction. Lastly, we can do far better with our papers than by sending them free to the same person continually. Lists of names are obtained from exchanges, of the principal men in western towns and a copy of THE COW BOY is sent to each one. As a consequence we have already reached thousands of people and made THE COW BOY at least as well known as any paper in the northwest.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy will go only to paying subscribers after this issue.

articles.text: The Marquis, his wife and party returned from Helena and Miles City Monday evening. After a stop of a few days they will go to St. Paul.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores and party return from Helena and Miles City.

articles.text: Justice Mark Bateman, H. G. Voss and Pat Cuskelley, all of Mandan, came up Tuesday to hold the inquest on the remains of John Magranahan.
articles.summary: Mandan officials come up for the Magranahan inquest.

articles.text: The site for the freight warehouse has been selected. It is on the south side of the track near the bluff. Work will begin as soon as the brick can be supplied by Mr. Book.
articles.summary: Freight warehouse site chosen south of the track.

articles.text: The frame to the new billiard hall is almost ready to raise, but work has been interrupted by the storm. An increased force has been put on and the work will be prosecuted as fast as possible.
articles.summary: Billiard hall work delayed by storm.

articles.text: The N. P. Ref. Car Co., in consonance with their advertisement, are now selling corn-fed beef. As a rule, range cattle are now too poor to kill, it paying better to delay killing till they increase in weight.
articles.summary: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. selling corn-fed beef.

articles.text: W. B. Wright and Mr. Baird arrived from New York Tuesday evening. Mr. Wright will soon leave for the east and Mr. Baird will remain and take charge of the Little Missouri Land and Stock Co.'s interests.
articles.summary: W. B. Wright and Baird arrive for the Little Missouri Land and Stock Co.

articles.text: George Wilkes returned last Friday evening from Chicago. He has brought along a number of tools and can now do the company's repairing, instead of having it sent way. That Mr. Wilkes is an able machinist, his work here abundantly shows.
articles.summary: Machinist George Wilkes back from Chicago with tools.

articles.text: Had it not been for the snow, Pennell & Roberts' outfit would now be loaded with Black Hills freight and on the road. There are now about 60,000 pounds here, which will make heavy enough load for the first trip. The outfit will start as soon as the weather permits loading.
articles.summary: Snow delays Pennell & Roberts' first Black Hills freight train.

articles.text: Z. Hyde returned from Chicago Saturday evening, accompanied by his wife and children. They are now keeping house at the Cantonment. Mr. Hyde will soon be in his glory handling the immense business that will be done at the abattoir this summer. The works will begin on full time very soon.
articles.summary: Z. Hyde returns with family; abattoir to start full time.

articles.text: The friends of T. J. Kerr will be happy to know that he has been promoted. Since his arrival, he has shown his bookkeeping ability so thoroughly that he has now been appointed traveling auditor for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. At present, sets of books will be kept at twelve different places and he will have a general supervision over the whole. His headquarters will be here with those of the company.
articles.summary: T. J. Kerr made traveling auditor of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.

articles.text: The present snow-storm is a perfect blessing to the cattle men. Almost every particle of it will melt into the ground and give the grass the moisture it so much needs. The perfect weather of the last three weeks has dried out the ground too much and the present snow in this warm weather will do as much good as twice the amount of moisture in the form of rain. "'Tis an ill wind that blows nobody good."
articles.summary: Spring snow-storm welcomed by cattlemen.

articles.text: We publish this week the price-list of lots. The plat can be seen at THE COW BOY office. It will be seen that the prices are low, both because of the assured future of Medora and because of the limited number of lots. The prices are subject to change without notice and as the prices are at rock bottom an early investment before a raise in prices will pay the prospective purchaser. Terms will be made known at THE COW BOY office.
articles.summary: Price-list of Medora lots published.

articles.text: Wm. Huggins, of Scotland, has made up his mind to stay with us and go into business. He will go into some mercantile business with McNeave Nally in charge, and besides will go into the business of raising horses. He cannot possibly find a better location for both. The growth Medora is bound to undergo will make the first profitable and there is a constant demand for cow horses here that the home market cannot begin to supply.
articles.summary: Scotsman Wm. Huggins to open a store and raise horses.

articles.text: Last Saturday Messrs. Pennell, Roberts and Packard went out to the divide to stake the route through the Bad Lands. The completeness and perfection of the road are astonishing. The only hill worth mentioning is about two miles from Medora and at no season of the year will teams have to be doubled on it. The whole route is now complete and it only needs one bull-train to mark it thoroughly. Stakes were put up by the party on Saturday, but owing to illiteracy or something the plain direction, "Keep to the right and avoid the washout," was read by Messrs. Allen and Deffebach "Keep straight ahead and camp in the washout." Tuesday, at the request of the former, ninety large guide-boards were painted to be distributed along the route, and it now looks as though one could walk on them from here to the divide.
articles.summary: Pennell, Roberts and Packard stake the freight route to the divide; ninety guide-boards painted.

articles.text: Last Sunday morning as the train from the west was on the point of starting out, the dead body of a man was discovered on the north side of the track about a thousand feet east of the depot. Investigation showed that the head and arms had been severed from the body. The head lying on the opposite side of the track and about twenty feet west of the body. The man's name was John Magranahan and he had been cutting wood the past winter. He was a wanderer and no one seems to know where his home was. At present it is on the coal-mine butte. Tuesday evening a coroner's jury was impanelled, consisting of H. G. Voss, R. J. Jewell and M. M. Coleman. The evidence was heard before Justice Bateman, of Mandan. Not much farther testimony was brought out than the above except the manner of death. Geo. Fitzgerald's testimony was the clearest on this point and had most weight on account of his extended railroad experience. As there were almost no bruises on the body and the head and arms were cut off so smoothly it seemed manifest that the deceased was riding between the cars and falling off was run over by the wheels. There were no marks about the body to indicate that he had been struck by the pilot of an engine. Besides that the body was almost touching the rails when found. Had he been struck by the pilot he would have been thrown off the embankment. It was brought out in the evidence of the witnesses that the deceased had been seen as late as 10 o'clock Saturday night in an intoxicated condition. The body was buried Monday on the coal-mine butte.
articles.summary: Woodcutter John Magranahan found dead beside the track; a coroner's jury concluded he fell between the cars and was run over.

articles.text: We congratulate our citizens beforehand on the acquisition of one and perhaps two of the best citizens of the Hills. We allude to Messrs. Louthan and Jorgens. Dr. Louthan has the best practice in the Hills, but realizing that more money can be made here than by practicing anywhere, he will come. Mr. Jorgens does the largest drug business in the Hills and will open up a drug store here as soon as possible. They are both old timers and will make valuable citizens.
articles.summary: Dr. Louthan and druggist Jorgens of the Black Hills expected to settle in Medora.
